angina.name: Angina
angina.definition: Angina is chest pain or discomfort that happens when the heart muscle does not get enough blood.
angina.overview: Angina is chest discomfort caused by reduced blood flow to the heart. The NHS says it is usually due to coronary heart disease, where fatty deposits narrow the arteries that supply the heart. It is often brought on by physical effort or stress and tends to ease within a few minutes of rest. The British Heart Foundation describes four main types: stable, unstable, vasospastic and microvascular angina. The NHS describes angina as a warning sign of a risk of serious problems such as heart attacks and strokes.
causes: Narrowing of the arteries that supply the heart muscle, usually from a build-up of fatty deposits (coronary heart disease).
Spasm of a coronary artery, as in vasospastic angina.
riskFactors: High blood pressure or high cholesterol
signs: A GP may check blood pressure, BMI and cholesterol when angina is suspected.
An ECG records the heart's rhythm and electrical activity.
complications: Angina is a warning sign of a risk of serious problems such as heart attacks and strokes, according to the NHS.
Unstable angina carries a higher risk of a heart attack, according to the BHF.
angina.diagnosis: A GP may check blood pressure, BMI and cholesterol and ask about symptoms and family history. If angina is suspected, NHS 111 Wales says the person is referred to a heart specialist (cardiologist). Hospital tests listed by the NHS include an ECG, an exercise ECG, coronary angiography and blood tests.
angina.treatment: The NHS describes three main approaches: medicines to relieve attacks, medicines to prevent attacks, and surgery. For stable angina, the usual approach is a medicine used during an attack, glyceryl trinitrate (GTN), with other medicines to prevent attacks and reduce heart risk. Some people need surgery, such as angioplasty with a stent or a coronary artery bypass graft.
angina.prevention: The BHF lists stopping smoking, staying active and keeping weight, cholesterol, blood pressure and diabetes under control as central to managing angina. The NHS says avoiding triggers such as stress, cold weather and large meals can help prevent attacks.
angina.seekCare: Call 999 if chest pain does not ease after resting or after angina medicine, spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back, or comes with sweating, nausea, light-headedness or breathlessness. For chest pain that goes away within a few minutes, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment. Someone with chest pain on exertion that eases with rest and no diagnosis is advised to contact the GP practice.

sections.heading: What does angina feel like?
sections.body:
Chest pain could be angina if it feels tight, dull or heavy, spreads to the arms, neck, jaw or back, is triggered by physical effort or stress, and stops within a few minutes of rest, according to the NHS. Some people also have breathlessness, nausea or tiredness. Stable angina typically lasts five minutes or less.

Angina is often set off by physical effort or stress and tends to ease with rest or angina medicine. The NHS says avoiding triggers such as stress, cold temperatures and large meals can help prevent attacks. The BHF notes that angina is not a mini heart attack and generally does not leave lasting damage. A heart attack is different: its symptoms usually last longer and are not relieved by rest or by GTN spray.

Angina and heart attack symptoms can overlap. The BHF says angina-like symptoms that do not settle with rest or GTN could be the start of a heart attack, and the NHS advises calling 999 for an ambulance if symptoms do not stop within a few minutes.

sections.heading: What are the different types of angina?
sections.body:
The BHF describes four main types of angina. Stable angina is the most common. It is typically brought on by exertion and generally eases with rest or medicine. Unstable angina is less predictable. It can occur at rest, may not respond well to medicine, and carries a higher risk of a heart attack, according to the BHF.

Vasospastic angina, also called Prinzmetal's angina or variant angina, is caused by a coronary artery going into spasm. It usually comes on at rest, often in the early morning or at night, and people with it typically do not get angina during exercise.

Microvascular angina, also called cardiac syndrome X, affects the smallest coronary arteries and tends to appear under physical or emotional stress. The BHF notes that it can occur alongside vasospastic angina.

sections.heading: How is angina diagnosed?
sections.body:
According to the NHS, assessment starts with a GP, who asks about symptoms, lifestyle and family history. The GP measures blood pressure, calculates body mass index (BMI) from weight and height, measures waist size and takes blood to check cholesterol. NHS inform says the checks can include blood tests for diabetes or anaemia.

If a GP thinks someone may have angina, NHS 111 Wales says the person is referred to a heart specialist, called a cardiologist. Hospital tests listed by the NHS include an ECG, an exercise ECG, coronary angiography and blood tests. An ECG is a test that checks the heart's rhythm and electrical activity.

The US National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute notes that an ECG can help recognise types of angina and other serious heart problems, but the result may be normal even in someone who has angina. It also says tests can help rule out other conditions and show whether urgent medical attention is needed.

sections.heading: How is angina treated?
sections.body:
The NHS describes three main approaches: medicines to relieve attacks, medicines to prevent attacks, and surgery. Glyceryl trinitrate, known as GTN, is the usual medicine for an attack and comes as a mouth spray or tablets that dissolve under the tongue. The NHS says GTN works by widening blood vessels.

To prevent attacks, the NHS lists beta blockers, which slow the heart and reduce the force of its contraction, and calcium channel blockers, which widen the arteries. Low-dose aspirin, statins and ACE inhibitors are used to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke. NICE guidance for stable angina recommends offering either a beta blocker or a calcium channel blocker first, and says statin treatment is offered in line with its lipid guidance.

Some people need surgery. Coronary angioplasty with stenting widens a narrowed artery using a small tube called a stent. A coronary artery bypass graft reroutes blood around a blocked section using a vessel taken from elsewhere in the body. Common GTN side effects are headache, dizziness and facial flushing, and the NHS notes that stopping regular GTN may make angina worse.

sections.heading: When is chest pain an emergency?
sections.body:
The NHS says to call 999 if chest pain does not stop after resting for a few minutes or after taking angina medicine. It also lists pain that spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back, and chest pain with sweating, nausea, light-headedness or shortness of breath, as reasons to call 999. The NHS advises against driving oneself to A&E.

For chest pain that has not been diagnosed, the NHS advises stopping and resting, and calling 999 for an ambulance if symptoms do not stop within a few minutes. If the pain goes away within a few minutes, the NHS advises making an urgent GP appointment. Someone with chest pain on exertion that eases with rest and no diagnosis is advised to contact the GP practice.

Because angina and heart attack symptoms overlap, the NHS says that anyone who is unsure should call 999 for an ambulance.

faqs.q: Is angina the same as a heart attack?
faqs.a: No. The BHF says angina is not a mini heart attack and generally does not leave lasting damage. Angina usually eases within a few minutes of rest or GTN, while heart attack symptoms usually last longer and are not relieved by rest or GTN spray. Angina is also a signal of a greater risk of a heart attack, so the NHS advises calling 999 if symptoms do not stop within a few minutes.

faqs.q: Can angina be controlled?
faqs.a: The NHS says that with symptoms well controlled and healthy lifestyle changes, people can usually have a normal life with angina, and that with treatment symptoms should improve over time and may eventually stop. Treatment includes medicines to relieve and prevent attacks, and some people need surgery such as angioplasty or a bypass graft.

faqs.q: What does GTN do?
faqs.a: GTN (glyceryl trinitrate) is the usual medicine for an angina attack, according to the NHS. It comes as a mouth spray or tablets that dissolve under the tongue and works by widening blood vessels. The NHS lists headache, dizziness and facial flushing as common side effects, and notes that stopping regular GTN may make angina worse.

faqs.q: When should chest pain prompt a 999 call?
faqs.a: The NHS says to call 999 if chest pain does not stop after resting for a few minutes or after angina medicine, spreads to the arm, neck, jaw or back, or comes with sweating, nausea, light-headedness or shortness of breath. For chest pain that goes away within a few minutes, the NHS advises an urgent GP appointment. Anyone unsure whether symptoms are angina or a heart attack should call 999.

diverticulitis.name: Diverticular disease and diverticulitis
diverticulitis.definition: Diverticular disease is a condition in which small pouches in the wall of the large intestine cause symptoms, and diverticulitis is when those pouches become inflamed or infected.
diverticulitis.overview: Diverticula are small pouches that bulge out of the wall of the large intestine. Pouches are common as people get older, and most people with them have no symptoms. When the pouches cause symptoms, doctors use the term diverticular disease. Diverticulitis, in which the pouches become inflamed or infected, most often causes abdominal pain, which is usually severe. Possible complications include an abscess, a blockage, a hole in the bowel, bleeding and fistulas.
causes: Small pouches form and bulge out of the wall of the large intestine.
Experts are not sure what causes diverticular disease and diverticulitis.
Diverticulitis happens when the pouches become inflamed or infected.
riskFactors: A diet low in fibre and high in red meat, which may be linked to higher risk
Genes may make some people more likely to develop the disease
signs: In severe illness, signs of sepsis such as confusion or pale, blotchy skin
complications: Bleeding
An abscess, a pus-filled cavity
A hole (perforation) in the bowel
A blockage of the bowel
A fistula, an abnormal connection between the bowel and another organ such as the bladder
diverticulitis.diagnosis: Doctors review the person's history, carry out a physical examination and order tests. Doctors may order blood tests, a stool test, imaging tests (typically a CT scan) and a colonoscopy, which may be recommended to confirm a diagnosis and rule out other conditions such as cancer. NICE offers a full blood count and C-reactive protein test to people with suspected complicated diverticulitis who are referred for same-day hospital assessment.
diverticulitis.treatment: The NHS says a high-fibre diet can often ease symptoms of diverticular disease, and paracetamol can be used to relieve pain. Mild diverticulitis can usually be treated at home with antibiotics prescribed by a GP, and more serious cases may need hospital care, usually with intravenous antibiotics. Surgery to remove the affected section of bowel is sometimes recommended after serious complications, although this is rare.
diverticulitis.prevention: The NHS lists increasing fibre slowly, drinking plenty of water, stopping smoking and keeping a healthy weight among the things people can do. MedlinePlus says whether a low-fibre diet leads to this problem is not well proven.
diverticulitis.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, being unable to pass stool or wind, heavy bleeding from the bottom, or signs of sepsis such as confusion, pale or blotchy skin or fast breathing. An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, tummy pain that is getting worse or not going away, a high temperature, or repeated vomiting that stops fluids staying down.

sections.heading: What is the difference between diverticulosis, diverticular disease and diverticulitis?
sections.body:
The word diverticula describes small pouches that form in the wall of the large intestine, which is also called the bowel. Having the pouches, known as diverticulosis, usually causes no discomfort, and most people with them never notice. Sometimes they are found by chance during tests done for another reason.

Diverticular disease is the term used when the pouches cause symptoms. It can cause constipation, diarrhoea, abdominal pain or bloating. Diverticulitis is the stage in which the pouches become inflamed or infected, as the NHS describes it.

NIDDK, a United States institute, says experts are not sure what causes these conditions. It says research suggests that certain genes may make some people more likely to develop diverticular disease. NIDDK also says diverticulosis is quite common, especially as people age, and NHS inform says most people with pouches have no symptoms.

sections.heading: What does diverticulitis feel like?
sections.body:
Diverticulitis most often causes abdominal pain, which is usually severe. The NHS lists severe, constant tummy pain and a high temperature among the symptoms, alongside constipation, diarrhoea, bloating and blood in the stool. Diverticular disease can also cause constipation, diarrhoea, abdominal pain or bloating.

Complications can include an abscess, a blockage, a hole in the bowel, bleeding and fistulas. NHS inform describes an abscess as a pus-filled cavity, and a fistula as an abnormal connection between the bowel and another organ such as the bladder.

NHS inform says surgery to remove the affected section of bowel is sometimes recommended after serious complications, although this is rare. Tummy pain that is getting worse or not going away, a high temperature, or blood in the stool are features for which the NHS advises getting urgent advice.

sections.heading: How do doctors diagnose diverticulitis?
sections.body:
Doctors start with the person's history and a physical examination. NIDDK says they may then order blood tests, a stool test, imaging tests and a colonoscopy. Imaging is typically a CT scan. A colonoscopy may be recommended to confirm a diagnosis of diverticular disease and to rule out other conditions, such as cancer.

NIDDK also says doctors ask about symptoms, bowel habits, what the person eats and drinks, medical conditions and medicines. Pouches are often found by chance during tests done for other reasons.

For people with suspected complicated acute diverticulitis who are referred for same-day hospital assessment, NICE guideline NG147 offers a full blood count, a urea and electrolytes test and a C-reactive protein test. The NICE committee called contrast CT the gold standard diagnostic test for acute diverticulitis and its complications.

sections.heading: How is diverticulitis treated?
sections.body:
Treatment depends on whether the problem is diverticular disease or diverticulitis and on how unwell the person is. The NHS says a high-fibre diet can often ease symptoms of diverticular disease, and paracetamol can be used to relieve pain.

For diverticulitis, the NHS says mild cases can usually be treated at home with antibiotics prescribed by a GP, while more serious cases may need hospital care, usually with intravenous antibiotics.

NICE guideline NG147 sets out different routes. People who are unwell all over the body but do not need referral are offered antibiotics by mouth. Those admitted to hospital with suspected complicated diverticulitis are offered antibiotics through a vein. Where a CT scan confirms uncomplicated acute diverticulitis, NICE says the need for antibiotics is reviewed, taking account of other medical conditions.

NICE recommends against offering antibiotics or an aminosalicylate medicine to prevent diverticulitis from coming back.

sections.heading: Can diet and lifestyle make a difference?
sections.body:
The NHS self-care advice includes increasing fibre slowly, drinking plenty of water, stopping smoking and keeping a healthy weight. It also says NSAID painkillers such as ibuprofen and opioids such as codeine can cause stomach problems or constipation and raise the risk of a bowel perforation.

MedlinePlus says providers may recommend a diet high in fibre and low in red meat, regular physical activity and not smoking. However, it also states that whether a low-fibre diet leads to the problem is not well proven.

Reviews on the NIH library site link low-fibre, high-red-meat diets, obesity, smoking, inactivity and regular NSAID use with higher risk. NIDDK says NSAIDs may increase the chance of diverticulitis complications.

Researchers are studying whether changes in gut bacteria and immune responses play a role, but a cause has not been established.

sections.heading: When should I get help for tummy pain or a high temperature?
sections.body:
The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, or being unable to pass stool or wind. The same applies to heavy bleeding from the bottom and to signs of sepsis, such as confusion, pale or blotchy skin, or fast breathing.

An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised for blood or mucus in the stool, tummy pain that is getting worse or not going away, a high temperature, or repeated vomiting that stops fluids staying down.

NHS inform lists reasons for hospital admission, including pain that paracetamol cannot control, being unable to drink enough fluids, being unable to take antibiotics by mouth, suspected complications, or no improvement after two days at home.

faqs.q: Is diverticulitis the same as diverticulosis?
faqs.a: No. Diverticulosis means having the small pouches in the wall of the large intestine, which usually causes no symptoms. Diverticular disease is the term used when the pouches cause symptoms or problems. Diverticulitis is when the pouches become inflamed or infected.

faqs.q: Does diverticulitis always need antibiotics?
faqs.a: NICE guideline NG147 offers antibiotics by mouth to people who are unwell all over the body but not referred to hospital. People in hospital with suspected complicated diverticulitis are offered antibiotics through a vein. Where a CT scan confirms uncomplicated acute diverticulitis, NICE says the need for antibiotics is reviewed, taking account of other medical conditions.

faqs.q: Which painkillers does the NHS mention for diverticular disease?
faqs.a: The NHS lists painkillers such as paracetamol among the treatments for diverticular disease symptoms. It says NSAIDs such as ibuprofen, and opioids such as codeine, can cause stomach problems or constipation and raise the risk of a bowel perforation. A GP can advise on the right choice for an individual.

faqs.q: Can diet prevent diverticular disease?
faqs.a: Experts are not sure what causes it, according to NIDDK. MedlinePlus lists diets low in fibre and high in red meat among lifestyle factors, and says providers may recommend a diet high in fibre and low in red meat. MedlinePlus also says it is not well proven that a low-fibre diet leads to the condition.

faqs.q: Is diverticulitis an emergency?
faqs.a: It can be. The NHS advises calling 999 for severe tummy pain with vomiting, a swollen tummy, being unable to pass stool or wind, heavy bleeding from the bottom or signs of sepsis. For blood or mucus in the stool, worsening pain, a high temperature or repeated vomiting, it advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111.

fatty-liver-disease.name: Fatty liver disease (MASLD)
fatty-liver-disease.definition: A common condition in which fat builds up in the liver, often linked to being overweight.
fatty-liver-disease.overview: Fatty liver disease linked to metabolic problems is now called MASLD and was formerly known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). The NHS says it is a common condition that can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes. It does not usually cause symptoms and is often found when tests done for another reason show a problem with the liver. The British Liver Trust says that in some people it can progress to scarring, and in a small number to cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer.
causes: Fat builds up in the liver, often in people who are overweight.
Experts are still studying the causes; NIDDK names certain health problems and genes among possible contributors.
signs: Yellow skin and eyes (jaundice), itchy skin, or swelling of the legs, ankles, feet or tummy, when cirrhosis has developed
complications: Inflammation of the liver (MASH, formerly NASH)
Scarring of the liver (fibrosis)
Cirrhosis, the most advanced stage
Liver failure and liver cancer in a small number of people
fatty-liver-disease.diagnosis: The NHS says fatty liver disease can be diagnosed using blood tests and sometimes an ultrasound scan of the tummy. An NHS trust page says a GP may order further blood tests, and sometimes an ultrasound scan, to confirm fat in the liver, rule out other causes and check for liver damage. NIDDK says doctors may use blood tests, imaging tests and a liver biopsy to diagnose the disease and to tell simple fatty liver from the inflamed form. NICE recommends that people with the condition are offered testing for advanced liver fibrosis. It also says the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test can be considered.
fatty-liver-disease.treatment: The NHS describes healthy lifestyle change as the core treatment. When there is scarring of the liver, the NHS says a liver specialist may prescribe pioglitazone or vitamin E.
fatty-liver-disease.prevention: The British Liver Trust says eating healthily, being physically active and staying at a healthy weight reduce the amount of fat in the liver. The NHS also advises not smoking.
fatty-liver-disease.seekCare: The NHS says a person with diagnosed cirrhosis who has yellow skin or eyes, or swelling in the tummy, legs, ankles or feet, should ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111. The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for vomiting blood, very dark or black tarry stools, or periods of confusion or drowsiness. MedlinePlus advises seeing a health care provider for unusual symptoms such as fatigue or abdominal pain.

sections.heading: What is fatty liver disease?
sections.body:
Fatty liver disease means fat has built up in the liver. The NHS describes it as a common condition that is often linked to being overweight and can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes. It was long called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or NAFLD. The British Liver Trust says metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, or MASLD, will replace that name, and that some pages still use the older one.

The British Liver Trust describes MASH as the more serious form. MedlinePlus says NASH is now called MASH. NIDDK distinguishes simple fatty liver from the inflamed form, NASH, and describes both as part of the same disease. The British Liver Trust says that in some people MASLD can progress to liver scarring, called fibrosis. It says that in a small number of people it can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer. NIDDK notes that experts are still studying the causes, and names certain health problems and genes among possible contributors.

sections.heading: Does fatty liver disease cause symptoms?
sections.body:
The NHS says fatty liver disease does not usually cause any symptoms. NIDDK calls NAFLD and NASH most often silent diseases with few or no symptoms. An NHS trust page says the condition is often found when blood tests or scans done for another reason show a problem with the liver.

Some people do have symptoms. The NHS lists feeling very tired, feeling generally unwell, and pain or discomfort under the right side of the ribs. MedlinePlus lists fatigue and pain in the upper right abdomen as the most common symptoms when they do appear.

NHS 111 Wales describes jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), itchy skin and swelling of the legs, ankles, feet or tummy as symptoms of cirrhosis, the most advanced stage. NIDDK warns, on its page for children, that once symptoms arise a child may already have permanent liver damage.

sections.heading: How is fatty liver disease diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says fatty liver disease can be diagnosed using blood tests and sometimes an ultrasound scan of the tummy. An NHS trust page says a GP may order further blood tests, and sometimes an ultrasound scan, to confirm fat in the liver, to rule out other causes and to check for liver damage. NIDDK says doctors may use blood tests, imaging tests and a liver biopsy to diagnose the disease and to tell simple fatty liver from the inflamed form.

Fibrosis means scarring of the liver. NICE recommends that people with the condition are offered testing for advanced liver fibrosis. It also says the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test can be considered, and it advises against using routine liver blood tests on their own to assess for advanced fibrosis. NICE advises that adults and young people diagnosed with advanced fibrosis are referred to a specialist in hepatology, the branch of medicine that deals with the liver.

sections.heading: How is fatty liver disease treated?
sections.body:
The NHS describes healthy lifestyle change as the core treatment. It advises a healthy balanced diet, regular exercise, weight loss for people who are overweight, limiting alcohol and not smoking. The British Liver Trust says losing weight and eating a healthy diet is the first line of treatment. It says eating healthily, being physically active and staying at a healthy weight reduce the amount of fat in the liver, which can slow down, stop and even reverse MASLD and MASH. NIDDK names weight loss as the main recommendation.

An NHS trust page says that without liver damage, lifestyle changes are generally the only treatment needed. When there is scarring of the liver, the NHS says a liver specialist may prescribe pioglitazone or vitamin E. MedlinePlus, a US source, describes a medicine called resmetirom, used with diet and exercise, for adults with NASH without cirrhosis who have moderate to advanced scarring.

sections.heading: How is fatty liver disease linked to type 2 diabetes?
sections.body:
The NHS lists type 2 diabetes among the factors linked to fatty liver disease, together with polycystic ovary syndrome and being over 50. It says the risk is higher in people who are overweight or have an unhealthy diet.

NIDDK says that in people with NAFLD, type 2 diabetes and being overweight or having obesity are key risk factors for simple fatty liver progressing to NASH and fibrosis. A review reports that diabetes promotes progression from simple fatty liver to NASH and increases the risk of cirrhosis and liver cancer.

The British Liver Trust says that in some people fatty liver disease progresses to scarring, and in a small number to cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer.

sections.heading: When should a person get help?
sections.body:
The NHS says a person with diagnosed cirrhosis who has yellow skin or eyes, or swelling in the tummy, legs, ankles or feet, should ask for an urgent GP appointment or contact NHS 111. NHS 111 Wales gives similar advice for people with fatty liver disease and a liver condition who have jaundice, itchy skin or swelling.

The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for vomiting blood, very dark or black tarry stools, or periods of confusion or drowsiness, particularly when cirrhosis has been diagnosed.

MedlinePlus advises seeing a health care provider for unusual symptoms such as fatigue or abdominal pain.

faqs.q: Can fatty liver disease be reversed?
faqs.a: The NHS says fatty liver disease can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes. The British Liver Trust says eating healthily, being active and staying at a healthy weight reduce liver fat, which can slow down, stop and even reverse MASLD and MASH. NIDDK says weight loss can reduce liver fat, inflammation and scarring. When there is fibrosis or cirrhosis, a liver specialist may be involved.

faqs.q: Is MASLD the same as NAFLD?
faqs.a: MASLD is the newer name for what was called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or NAFLD. The British Liver Trust says MASLD will replace the older name and that some pages still use it. The more serious inflamed form, MASH, was previously called NASH, and MedlinePlus says NASH is now called MASH.

faqs.q: Who is more likely to get fatty liver disease?
faqs.a: The NHS lists type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome and being over 50, and says the risk is higher in people who are overweight or have an unhealthy diet. NIDDK says type 2 diabetes and being overweight or having obesity are key risk factors for progression to NASH and fibrosis. Its children's page adds that genes may also play a part.

faqs.q: What tests are used to look for it?
faqs.a: The NHS says blood tests and sometimes an ultrasound scan of the tummy can be used. NIDDK says doctors may also use other imaging tests and a liver biopsy. NICE recommends that people with the condition are offered testing for advanced liver fibrosis, and says the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test can be considered.

influenza.name: Flu (influenza)
influenza.definition: Flu is a respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses.
influenza.overview: Flu is an infection caused by influenza viruses. It comes on very quickly, with a sudden high temperature, aching body, tiredness, dry cough, sore throat and headache. Most people have a mild illness, but flu can lead to complications such as bronchitis and pneumonia, and older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with long-term conditions are at higher risk. The NHS says having the vaccine before the flu season starts is the best way to avoid catching and spreading flu.
causes: Infection with influenza viruses; types A and B cause the seasonal epidemics seen in people.
The virus spreads mainly in droplets made when people with flu cough, sneeze or talk.
The WHO says the virus can also be spread by hands contaminated with influenza viruses.
NHS inform says germs from coughs and sneezes can survive on hands and surfaces for 24 hours.
riskFactors: Long-term conditions such as asthma, diabetes or heart disease
signs: A sudden high temperature, aching body and dry cough
complications: Bronchitis
Pneumonia
Sinus and ear infections
Inflammation of the heart or brain
Worsening of long-term conditions such as asthma and heart disease
In some cases, treatment in hospital
influenza.diagnosis: Flu can be confirmed with a test on a swab from the nose or throat. MedlinePlus describes rapid antigen tests as the most common flu tests but says they are not as accurate as other types. It describes molecular laboratory tests as the most accurate type of flu test.
influenza.treatment: Most people recover at home with rest, plenty of fluids and paracetamol or ibuprofen to lower a temperature and ease aches. GPs do not recommend antibiotics for flu, because it is caused by viruses. Antiviral medicines are prescription-only; the CDC recommends prompt treatment for people at higher risk of complications and says they work best when started within about two days. The NHS says aspirin should not be given to children under 16.
influenza.prevention: The NHS says having the vaccine before the flu season starts is the best way to avoid catching and spreading flu. NHS advice also includes washing hands often with warm water and soap, binning used tissues quickly, and covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing.
influenza.seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, difficulty breathing or coughing up a lot of blood. An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised when someone with flu symptoms is 65 or over, pregnant, has a long-term condition or a weakened immune system, or has not improved after 7 days. The CDC says most people with flu have a mild illness and do not need medical care.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of flu, and how is it different from a cold?
sections.body:
The NHS lists the main symptoms of flu as a sudden high temperature, an aching body, tiredness, a dry cough, a sore throat and a headache. Flu comes on very quickly. In children the symptoms are similar, but they can also have ear pain, sore eyes and swollen glands, and may seem less active, according to NHS England.

The CDC compares the two illnesses side by side. Flu typically starts abruptly, while cold symptoms build gradually. Tiredness and weakness are usual with flu but only sometimes happen with a cold.

Most people feel better within about a week, according to the CDC, although a cough and tiredness can last for a few more weeks. The CDC also says most people with flu have a mild illness and do not need medical care.

sections.heading: How does flu spread?
sections.body:
Flu is caused by influenza viruses. The CDC says there are four types, but influenza A and B viruses are the ones that circulate and cause seasonal epidemics. Type A viruses are grouped into subtypes, and A(H1N1) and A(H3N2) are currently circulating in humans.

The CDC says most experts believe flu spreads mainly through droplets made when people with the infection cough, sneeze or talk. The WHO adds that the virus can also be spread by hands contaminated with influenza viruses. NHS inform says germs from coughs and sneezes can survive on hands and surfaces for 24 hours.

The CDC says the incubation period is about two days, ranging from one to four days. People are most contagious during the first three days of illness, and young children and people with weakened immune systems may be contagious for longer.

sections.heading: How is flu diagnosed?
sections.body:
Flu can be confirmed with a rapid or laboratory test on a swab. MedlinePlus describes a standard test in which a clinician rotates a nasopharyngeal swab for 10 to 15 seconds before the sample is tested for influenza A and B. The CDC says rapid tests can use nasopharyngeal, nasal or throat swabs.

MedlinePlus says rapid antigen tests are the most common flu tests but are not as accurate as other types. Rapid molecular tests can give results quickly, and molecular laboratory tests are the most accurate type of flu test, although results can take up to three days.

The CDC also says that most people with flu have a mild illness and do not need medical care or antiviral drugs.

sections.heading: What is the treatment for flu?
sections.body:
Most people recover at home. NHS sources describe rest, sleep, warmth and plenty of water to avoid dehydration, with paracetamol or ibuprofen to lower a temperature and ease aches and pains. The NHS says aspirin should not be given to children under 16, and its Reye's syndrome page links that serious condition to aspirin use in this age group.

GPs do not recommend antibiotics for flu. Flu is caused by viruses, and antibiotics will not relieve symptoms or speed up recovery.

Antiviral medicines such as oseltamivir and zanamivir are available on prescription only. An NHS Borders leaflet says most people will not need them because their illness is mild and they recover quickly. The CDC recommends prompt treatment for people at higher risk of serious complications. It says antivirals work best when started within about two days, although a later start may still help people at higher risk or who are very sick.

sections.heading: What are the complications of flu, and when should someone get medical help?
sections.body:
The CDC lists pneumonia, bronchitis, sinus infections and ear infections among the complications of flu. It also lists inflammation of the heart and brain, and says flu can make chronic conditions such as asthma and heart disease worse. One NHS hospital page notes that some cases need treatment in hospital.

The CDC names young children, adults aged 65 and over, pregnant women and people with conditions such as asthma, chronic lung disease, diabetes or heart disease as being at higher risk of serious flu complications.

NHS England advises calling 999 or going to A&E for sudden chest pain, difficulty breathing or coughing up a lot of blood. It advises an urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 when someone with flu symptoms is 65 or over, pregnant, has a long-term condition or a weakened immune system, or has symptoms that do not improve after 7 days.

sections.heading: Who is offered the flu vaccine, and what else helps prevent flu?
sections.body:
The NHS says having the vaccine before the flu season starts is the best way to avoid catching and spreading flu. Protection is not guaranteed, but any flu after vaccination is typically milder, according to the NHS vaccine page.

NHS England says the free vaccine is offered to adults aged 65 and over, adults aged 18 to 64 with certain long-term health conditions, and pregnant women.

UKHSA's guide to the autumn 2026 programme also lists children, residents of long-stay care homes, close contacts of people with a weakened immune system, carers on Carer's Allowance and some frontline social care workers. The clinical risk groups include chronic respiratory disease, chronic heart disease, chronic liver disease, diabetes and a weakened immune system. Start dates differ between groups, so the UKHSA guide and NHS pages hold the current details.

faqs.q: Is flu the same as a cold?
faqs.a: They are different illnesses. The CDC says flu typically starts abruptly, while cold symptoms build gradually. It also says tiredness and weakness are usual with flu but only sometimes happen with a cold. The NHS lists the main flu symptoms as a sudden high temperature, an aching body, tiredness, a dry cough, a sore throat and a headache.

faqs.q: Do antibiotics work for flu?
faqs.a: No. GPs do not recommend antibiotics for flu, because flu is caused by viruses and antibiotics will not relieve symptoms or speed recovery. Antiviral medicines are prescription-only; the CDC recommends prompt treatment for people at higher risk and says they work best when started within about two days. Most people recover with rest, fluids and simple pain relief.

faqs.q: How long is someone contagious with flu?
faqs.a: The CDC says people with flu are most contagious during the first three days of illness, and the incubation period is about two days, ranging from one to four days. Young children and people with weakened immune systems may be contagious for longer. NHS England says people are most likely to pass flu on in the first five days.

faqs.q: Who is most at risk of serious illness from flu?
faqs.a: The CDC names young children, people aged 65 and over, pregnant women and people with conditions such as asthma, chronic lung disease, diabetes or heart disease as being at higher risk of serious flu complications. People with a weakened immune system are also included in UKHSA's clinical risk groups for the flu vaccine.

faqs.q: When does flu need emergency help?
faqs.a: NHS England advises calling 999 or going to A&E for sudden chest pain, difficulty breathing or coughing up a lot of blood. An urgent GP appointment or NHS 111 is advised for people aged 65 or over, who are pregnant, or who have a long-term condition or weakened immune system, and for anyone whose symptoms have not improved after 7 days.

irritable-bowel-syndrome.name: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)
irritable-bowel-syndrome.definition: A long-term digestive condition with repeated abdominal pain and changes in bowel habit, but no visible damage or disease in the digestive tract.
irritable-bowel-syndrome.overview: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common long-term condition of the digestive system. It causes stomach cramps, bloating, diarrhoea and constipation, and these symptoms tend to come and go. The NHS says it is usually a lifelong problem, although changes to diet and lifestyle and medicines can help. The exact cause is unknown. MedlinePlus says it affects about twice as many women as men and is most often found in people younger than 45.
causes: The exact cause is unknown.
It has been linked to food moving through the gut too quickly or too slowly.
It has been linked to oversensitive nerves in the gut.
Experts think problems with brain-gut interaction may play a part.
Stress and a family history of IBS have also been linked to it.
riskFactors: Gastroenteritis (a gut infection) is listed by NHS inform among the things IBS has been linked to
Being female: about twice as many women as men are affected
Flare-up triggers include alcohol, caffeine, spicy or fatty foods, stress and anxiety, and regular antibiotic use
signs: Often no visible sign of damage or disease in the digestive tract
Examination may check for warning features such as unexplained weight loss, rectal bleeding or lumps in the tummy, which prompt further investigation
complications: IBS can be painful, but it does not damage the digestive tract
One cross-sectional survey found people with self-reported IBS reported more diet-related anxiety and worry than people without IBS
irritable-bowel-syndrome.diagnosis: There is no test that confirms IBS. A doctor can usually diagnose it from the typical symptoms. Tests are used to rule out other conditions. A GP may arrange a blood test for coeliac disease and stool tests for infection or inflammatory bowel disease. NICE guidance suggests considering IBS when a person has abdominal pain or discomfort, bloating or a change in bowel habit. Assessment includes looking for red flag features, and a positive diagnosis can be made once these and other causes such as coeliac disease are ruled out.
irritable-bowel-syndrome.treatment: Diet and lifestyle changes are the first step, and medicines can be considered if these do not control symptoms. The choice of medicine depends on the main symptom: antispasmodics or peppermint oil for pain and bloating, loperamide for diarrhoea, and laxatives for constipation. Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants are sometimes used for pain. Cognitive behavioural therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy are other options. A low FODMAP diet is described as best followed with support from a dietitian, and a GP can refer to one.
irritable-bowel-syndrome.prevention: The NHS lists alcohol, caffeine, spicy or fatty foods, stress and anxiety and regular antibiotic use as triggers of flare-ups. NHS trust self-help guides describe keeping a food and symptom diary, regular exercise and managing stress.
irritable-bowel-syndrome.seekCare: The NHS suggests seeing a GP when IBS may be the cause and symptoms have lasted more than 4 weeks. NHS inform advises contacting the GP urgently for a change in bowel habit lasting more than 6 weeks, especially over the age of 50, or for unexplained weight loss, a lump in the tummy or back passage, or bleeding from the back passage.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of IBS?
sections.body:
The main symptoms of IBS are stomach pain or cramps, bloating, diarrhoea and constipation. Some people have mostly diarrhoea, some mostly constipation, and some have both. The NHS says symptoms tend to come and go, and an episode can last for days, weeks or months at a time. Other symptoms the NHS lists include wind, passing mucus with stools, tiredness, feeling sick, backache and pelvic pain.

NIDDK adds that a feeling of not having finished a bowel movement, and whitish mucus in the stool, can occur. It also says women with IBS often have more symptoms during their periods. IBS can be painful, but NIDDK says it does not damage the digestive tract. NHS inform says the symptoms are similar to those of coeliac disease and inflammatory bowel disease, so doctors rule those conditions out.

sections.heading: What causes IBS and what triggers flare-ups?
sections.body:
The NHS says the exact cause of IBS is not known. It has been linked to food moving through the gut too quickly or too slowly, oversensitive nerves in the gut, stress and a family history of IBS. NIDDK says experts think a combination of problems may lead to IBS, and that different factors may cause it in different people. One idea it describes is a problem with brain-gut interaction, which may change how fast food moves through the digestive tract. NHS inform also lists gastroenteritis, a gut infection with diarrhoea and vomiting, among the things IBS has been linked to.

Flare-ups can happen for no obvious reason, the NHS says. The common triggers it lists are alcohol, caffeine, spicy or fatty foods, stress and anxiety, and regular use of antibiotics. Keeping a food and symptom diary is one way described to spot personal triggers.

sections.heading: How is IBS diagnosed?
sections.body:
There is no single test for IBS, and doctors mostly rely on the pattern of symptoms. NICE guidance suggests considering IBS when a person has abdominal pain or discomfort, bloating or a change in bowel habit. Doctors check for red flag features, such as rectal bleeding or unexplained weight loss, and the NHS says the GP may also feel the tummy to check for lumps or swelling. If any red flags are present, NICE says the person should be referred for further investigation.

Tests are used mainly to rule out other conditions. A GP may order a blood test for coeliac disease and stool tests for infection or inflammatory bowel disease. NICE says faecal calprotectin testing is an option to help tell inflammatory bowel disease from IBS in adults. Once warning features and other causes such as coeliac disease are ruled out, a positive diagnosis of IBS can be made. NIDDK notes that IBS shows no visible signs of damage or disease in the digestive tract.

sections.heading: How is IBS treated?
sections.body:
Guidance describes diet and lifestyle measures as the first step, with medicines considered if these do not control symptoms. Self-help described in NHS trust guides includes keeping a food and symptom diary, taking regular exercise and finding ways to manage stress. NICE says healthcare professionals should review fibre intake, and that insoluble fibre such as bran should be discouraged. A low FODMAP diet is described as best followed with support from a dietitian, and a GP can refer to one. NIDDK describes FODMAPs as carbohydrates that are hard to digest.

The choice of medicine depends on the main symptom. Antispasmodics can ease abdominal pain, peppermint oil may help bloating, and loperamide is used for diarrhoea. Laxatives are used for constipation. Low-dose tricyclic antidepressants are sometimes used for pain. NIDDK lists cognitive behavioural therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy as mental health therapies for IBS, and NHS talking therapy services offer CBT for IBS.

sections.heading: Who gets IBS and when should it be checked by a doctor?
sections.body:
MedlinePlus says IBS is common, affects about twice as many women as men, and is most often found in people younger than 45. NIDDK gives a slightly different age picture, saying people younger than 50 are more likely to develop IBS than people older than 50.

The NHS suggests seeing a GP if IBS may be the cause and symptoms have lasted more than 4 weeks. NHS inform advises contacting the GP urgently for a change in bowel habit lasting more than 6 weeks, especially over the age of 50, and for unexplained weight loss, a lump in the tummy or back passage, or bleeding from the back passage. NHS 111 Wales similarly says to ask for an urgent appointment after losing a lot of weight for no reason or bleeding from the bottom. These are among the red flag features clinicians check for before making a diagnosis of IBS.

faqs.q: Can IBS be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for IBS and that it is usually a lifelong problem. Symptoms tend to come and go, and changes to diet and lifestyle, together with medicines, can often help control them. Psychological treatments such as cognitive behavioural therapy and hypnotherapy are also options for some people.

faqs.q: Is IBS the same as inflammatory bowel disease?
faqs.a: They are different conditions, although NHS inform says the symptoms are similar, so inflammatory bowel disease has to be ruled out. Doctors may use blood and stool tests to help tell them apart. NIDDK says IBS shows no visible signs of damage or disease in the digestive tract. NICE says faecal calprotectin testing is an option to help tell inflammatory bowel disease from IBS in adults.

faqs.q: Does IBS damage the bowel?
faqs.a: NIDDK says IBS can be painful but does not damage the digestive tract. Doctors still look for warning features, such as rectal bleeding or unexplained weight loss. When these are present, NICE says the person should be referred for further investigation to find the cause.

faqs.q: Can stress cause IBS?
faqs.a: The NHS lists stress among the factors linked to IBS, and says stress and anxiety can trigger flare-ups. The exact cause is unknown, and NIDDK says different factors may cause IBS in different people. NHS inform also lists gastroenteritis, oversensitive nerves and food moving through the gut too quickly or too slowly among the linked factors.

faqs.q: Which foods trigger IBS symptoms?
faqs.a: The NHS lists alcohol, caffeine, and spicy or fatty foods as common triggers. A food and symptom diary is described as a way to spot personal triggers. A low FODMAP diet is described as best followed with support from a dietitian, and a GP can refer to one.

multiple-sclerosis.name: Multiple sclerosis (MS)
multiple-sclerosis.definition: A lifelong condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks nerves in the brain and spinal cord.
multiple-sclerosis.overview: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a lifelong condition that affects the brain and spinal cord. NINDS describes it as an autoimmune disease in which the immune system becomes misdirected and attacks healthy tissue, and says the cause is still unknown. The MS Society says symptoms can come and go and can change over time. NICE says symptoms usually begin in a person's 20s or 30s. There is currently no cure, but the NHS says treatments can slow progression and help ease symptoms.
causes: NINDS describes MS as an autoimmune disease in which the immune system becomes misdirected and attacks healthy tissue, and says the exact cause is still unknown.
NINDS says genetic alterations, environmental exposures and immunologic factors make the development of MS more likely.
NINDS reports that people with higher vitamin D levels or more sun exposure appear less likely to develop MS.
riskFactors: Epstein-Barr virus, which causes infectious mononucleosis, is the infection NINDS describes as most consistently linked to the development of MS.
People who smoke are more likely to develop MS and tend to have a more aggressive disease course, according to NINDS.
Lower vitamin D levels or less sun exposure, which NINDS links with a higher likelihood of MS.
Women are more likely than men to develop MS, according to NINDS.
signs: Areas of scar-like tissue, called lesions or plaques, in the brain and spinal cord, which result from the immune system attacking myelin and are visible on an MRI scan.
The return of old symptoms because of triggers, which an NHS trust describes as decompensation or pseudo-relapse.
complications: Worsening symptoms that lead to increased disability over time in some people.
Relapses, when new symptoms develop or existing symptoms worsen.
Bladder problems.
multiple-sclerosis.diagnosis: The NHS says there is no single test for MS. A GP who suspects MS refers the person to a neurologist, who asks about symptoms. MedlinePlus lists an MRI scan, blood tests to rule out other conditions, and a lumbar puncture among the tools used. NINDS says doctors can often diagnose MS from a person's symptoms and characteristic signs on an MRI scan.
multiple-sclerosis.treatment: There is currently no cure, but the NHS says treatments can slow progression and ease symptoms. Disease-modifying therapies can reduce the number and severity of relapses, and are only prescribed to people whose MS meets specific criteria. Steroids are used for relapses, and NICE says treatment for a relapse that would benefit from it should be offered within 14 days of symptoms starting. Symptom management can include muscle relaxants, physiotherapy and cognitive behavioural therapy, which the NHS says can help with anxiety, depression and fatigue.
multiple-sclerosis.prevention: NINDS says the cause of MS is still unknown, and the sources reviewed do not describe a proven way to prevent it. NINDS reports that people who smoke are more likely to develop MS.
multiple-sclerosis.seekCare: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden weakness or numbness in one arm, loss or blurring of vision, or problems with balance and coordination. For suspected MS symptoms, the NHS advises seeing a GP, who refers the person to a neurologist. For people already diagnosed, MedlinePlus lists reasons to contact a healthcare provider, including worsening pain, recent falls, and choking or coughing when eating.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of MS?
sections.body:
The NHS lists fatigue, blurred vision or eye pain, numbness or tingling, balance problems, bladder problems and difficulty with memory or concentration among the symptoms of MS. The MS Society says that symptoms can come and go and can change over time.

The MS Society explains that fatigue in MS is not just the ordinary tiredness that follows a hard day's work. It lists numbness and tingling among the common symptoms, and notes that tingling can last a few minutes or hours and can also be a sign of anxiety, so the pattern alone does not point to MS.

Heat can affect symptoms. The MS Society says some people feel worse when they are too hot or too cold, and it uses the name Uhthoff's phenomenon for the effect of heat, with symptoms usually going back to earlier levels as the body cools. MedlinePlus says fever, hot baths, sun exposure and stress can trigger or worsen attacks.

sections.heading: What are the types of MS, and what is a relapse?
sections.body:
The NHS describes three main types of MS: relapsing remitting, secondary progressive and primary progressive. Relapsing remitting is the most common pattern, with flare-ups followed by periods of improvement, and over time it often turns into secondary progressive MS. In secondary progressive MS, symptoms persist and gradually worsen. In primary progressive MS, symptoms steadily worsen from the start without periods of remission, and this form is less common.

NICE says a relapse is diagnosed when a person develops new symptoms or has worsening of existing symptoms that last more than 24 hours, in the absence of infection or any other cause, after a stable period of at least one month. NICE adds that infection, particularly urinary tract and respiratory infection, should be ruled out first.

An NHS trust describes the return of old symptoms because of triggers as decompensation or pseudo-relapse. It says this is not due to new inflammatory activity and that steroids are not helpful for it.

sections.heading: How is MS diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no single test for MS. If a GP thinks a person could have MS, the GP refers them to a neurologist, a specialist in the brain and nerves, who asks about their symptoms. NHS guidance lists blood tests to check for similar conditions, an MRI scan and a lumbar puncture among the tests that may be used.

NINDS describes the scar-like areas, called plaques or lesions, that result from the immune attack on myelin, and says they can be seen on an MRI scan. It adds that identifying this damage could allow a full diagnosis of MS even after a single attack.

NICE says its committee based the diagnostic recommendations on the McDonald criteria and stressed excluding fever and infection, which can mimic the symptoms of MS.

sections.heading: How is MS treated?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is currently no cure for MS, but treatments can slow its progression and help ease symptoms. The choice of medicine depends on the type of MS and the symptoms, and it often changes over time.

The NHS lists steroids for relapses and disease-modifying therapies, which reduce how often relapses happen and how severe they are. These therapies are only prescribed to people whose MS meets specific criteria, which for secondary progressive MS include the number of relapses. NINDS says steroids calm inflammation and speed recovery from attacks, but do not change the long-term course of the disease. NICE says adults with a relapse that would benefit from treatment should be offered it as soon as possible and within 14 days of symptoms starting.

NHS Scotland says symptom management covers fatigue, spasticity, bladder and bowel problems, pain and mental health, often with physiotherapy and other specialist support. The NHS says cognitive behavioural therapy can help with anxiety, depression and fatigue.

sections.heading: What is the outlook for someone with MS?
sections.body:
NICE describes MS as a permanent condition. It says MS affects approximately 130,000 people in the UK and is the most common cause of serious physical disability in adults of working age. NICE adds that symptoms usually begin in a person's 20s or 30s.

NINDS says most people with MS have a normal life expectancy. It reports that a small number of people have mild symptoms with little disability, while others have worsening symptoms that lead to increased disability over time. MedlinePlus likewise says life expectancy can be normal or almost normal. The MS Society notes that symptoms can come and go and can change over time.

NICE says there is currently no cure for MS, but many symptoms can be treated and there are medicines that can help people have fewer and less severe relapses.

sections.heading: When should someone get medical help for MS symptoms?
sections.body:
The NHS advises seeing a GP for anyone who thinks they have symptoms of MS. If the GP suspects MS, the person is referred to a neurologist, because there is no single test.

The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for sudden weakness or numbness in one arm, loss or blurring of vision, or problems with balance and coordination.

For people already diagnosed with MS, MedlinePlus lists reasons to contact a healthcare provider, including pain that is becoming worse, recent falls, and choking or coughing when eating. It also lists signs of a bladder infection, such as fever and burning when passing urine, as a reason to get in touch with a provider.

faqs.q: Can MS be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is currently no cure for MS, but treatments can slow progression and help ease symptoms. NICE's public information says it is possible to treat many of the symptoms, and that there are medicines that can help people have fewer and less severe relapses.

faqs.q: Who diagnoses multiple sclerosis?
faqs.a: The NHS says a GP who thinks a person could have MS refers them to a neurologist, and that there is no single test. The tests that may be used include an MRI scan, a lumbar puncture, and blood tests to check for other conditions that are similar to MS.

faqs.q: What is a relapse?
faqs.a: NICE says a relapse is when new symptoms develop or existing symptoms worsen for more than 24 hours, in the absence of infection or any other cause, after a stable period of at least one month. An NHS trust says the return of old symptoms because of triggers is called a pseudo-relapse, and that steroids are not helpful for it.

faqs.q: Does MS shorten life expectancy?
faqs.a: NINDS states that most people with MS have a normal life expectancy. It adds that a small number of people have mild symptoms with little disability, while others have worsening symptoms that lead to increased disability over time. The MS Society says symptoms can come and go and can change over time.

norovirus.name: Norovirus (vomiting bug)
norovirus.definition: A highly contagious viral infection of the gut that causes sudden vomiting and diarrhoea.
norovirus.overview: Norovirus is a very contagious stomach bug that causes vomiting and diarrhoea. Most people recover within a few days without specific treatment. Young children, older adults and people with other illnesses are at higher risk of dehydration. It spreads by direct contact with an infected person, through contaminated food or drink, and through contaminated surfaces.
causes: Infection with norovirus, which spreads mainly by the faecal-oral route.
Direct contact with an infected person.
Eating or drinking contaminated food or water.
Touching contaminated surfaces.
Shellfish such as oysters taken from polluted water, which can carry the virus.
Food contaminated during preparation.
riskFactors: Very young or older age, or other illness, which raise the risk of dehydration.
A weakened immune system, which raises the risk of dehydration.
Staying in hospitals or long-term care facilities, where outbreaks are commonly reported.
Close living quarters such as cruise ships, camps and dormitories.
signs: A high temperature in some people.
Signs of dehydration, such as dark urine, passing less urine than usual, or fewer wet nappies in babies.
complications: Dehydration, from fluid lost through vomiting and diarrhoea.
More severe or prolonged illness in some people, including older adults and those with weakened immune systems.
norovirus.diagnosis: Diagnosis is usually based on the symptoms. Stool test panels can detect norovirus.
norovirus.treatment: There is no specific cure or antiviral medicine, and antibiotics do not work because the cause is a virus. Care focuses on rest and drinking plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration. A pharmacist can supply oral rehydration powder when there are signs of dehydration.
norovirus.prevention: Washing hands with soap and water is the key measure, because alcohol-based hand gels do not inactivate the virus. UK guidance advises staying away from work, school and hospital or care home visits, and avoiding preparing food for others, until 48 hours after symptoms stop. The CDC says no norovirus vaccine is currently available.
norovirus.seekCare: The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E for blood in vomit, green vomit, a sudden severe headache or difficulty breathing, or for signs of shock from dehydration such as pale, blue or grey skin, confusion or being hard to wake. The NHS says to call NHS 111 if diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days, vomiting lasts more than 2 days, fluids cannot be kept down, there is blood in the diarrhoea, a baby is under 12 months, or a child under 5 shows signs of dehydration. A pharmacist can advise on oral rehydration, and UKHSA asks people with symptoms to phone a GP or NHS 111 rather than attend A&E or a surgery unless advised.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of norovirus?
sections.body:
The NHS says the main symptoms of norovirus usually start suddenly. They are feeling sick, being sick and diarrhoea. The CDC lists nausea, stomach pain, fever, headache and body aches among the symptoms, and says they usually start 12 to 48 hours after exposure.

The CDC says most people get better within one to three days. The NHS says symptoms typically last up to two or three days, and UKHSA says most people recover in two to three days without needing any medicine.

The CDC says frequent vomiting and diarrhoea can cause dehydration, which is most dangerous for young children, older adults and people with other illnesses. NHS pages describe signs such as dark yellow, strong-smelling urine, passing urine less often than usual and feeling dizzy or lightheaded. In babies, the signs include fewer wet nappies than usual. The CDC adds that children may cry with few or no tears.

sections.heading: How does norovirus spread?
sections.body:
The CDC says norovirus spreads mainly by the faecal-oral route, either through direct contact with an infected person or through contaminated food or drink. It can also spread when people touch contaminated surfaces and then put unwashed fingers in their mouths. CDC guidance gives an estimated infectious dose as low as 18 virus particles.

The CDC says people are most contagious while they are ill and in the few days after recovering, and that studies show some people can still spread the virus for two weeks or more after feeling better. UKHSA says people may still be shedding the virus for 48 hours after symptoms stop.

Shellfish such as oysters can carry norovirus when grown in polluted water, and the CDC advises cooking shellfish thoroughly. A CDC analysis found that most foodborne norovirus contamination happens during food preparation.

The CDC says outbreaks often occur where people live or gather closely, including hospitals, nursing homes and other long-term care facilities, cruise ships, camps, dormitories and hotels.

sections.heading: How is norovirus diagnosed and treated?
sections.body:
The CDC Yellow Book says norovirus infection is generally diagnosed from clinical symptoms. It also notes that stool test panels can detect the virus with good sensitivity and specificity.

The NHS says there is no specific medicine for norovirus and that the illness has to run its course. The CDC Yellow Book says antibiotics are not useful, and UKHSA says they do not work because norovirus is a virus. Care centres on resting and drinking plenty of fluids to prevent dehydration.

The NHS advises avoiding fruit juice and fizzy drinks, which can make diarrhoea worse, and says children under 12 should not be given medicine to stop diarrhoea. NHS guidance also says children under 16 should not be given aspirin.

For babies, NHS guidance says breastfeeding or bottle feeding can continue, formula should be made up at its usual strength, and smaller, more frequent feeds may help breastfed babies who are being sick. A pharmacist can recommend oral rehydration powder when there are signs of dehydration, and the CDC says oral rehydration fluids are most helpful for mild dehydration.

sections.heading: When should someone get help for the vomiting bug?
sections.body:
The NHS says to call 999 or go to A&E if vomit contains blood or looks like coffee grounds, or is green. It gives the same advice for a sudden severe headache, a stiff neck with sensitivity to light, severe tummy pain, confusion or difficulty breathing. Dehydration can also lead to shock, and the NHS says to call 999 for signs such as blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, severe difficulty breathing, confusion or being hard to wake.

The NHS says to call NHS 111 if diarrhoea lasts more than 7 days or vomiting lasts more than 2 days, if fluids cannot be kept down, or if there is blood in the diarrhoea. NHS 111 is also the route for concerns about a baby under 12 months, and for a child under 5 with signs of dehydration such as fewer wet nappies.

UKHSA asks people with symptoms not to go to A&E or a GP surgery unless advised to. Phoning the GP or NHS 111 is the suggested first step, and a pharmacist can advise on oral rehydration.

sections.heading: How can the spread of norovirus be reduced?
sections.body:
The NHS and CDC say washing hands with soap and water is the key measure, and that alcohol hand gels do not kill norovirus. The CDC also advises cleaning and disinfecting contaminated surfaces and washing laundry in hot water. UKHSA advises using bleach-based products on surfaces. NHS guidance says soiled clothes and bedding should be washed separately on the hottest cycle the fabric allows.

UKHSA advises staying at home until 48 hours after symptoms stop, and not preparing food for others during that time. The NHS and UKHSA also ask people who are unwell not to visit hospitals or care homes.

UK outbreak guidance for health and care settings describes keeping affected people apart, frequent cleaning of touched surfaces with chlorine-based products, and closing affected bays, wards or care homes to new admissions where appropriate.

The CDC says no norovirus vaccine or antiviral is currently available and that vaccine development is advancing.

faqs.q: Can you catch norovirus more than once?
faqs.a: The CDC outbreak guidelines say there is no long-lasting immunity to norovirus. The CDC also says no norovirus vaccine or antiviral drug is currently available. The measures the NHS and CDC describe for reducing spread are washing hands with soap and water and cleaning contaminated surfaces. The NHS and UKHSA say most people recover within a few days.

faqs.q: Do antibiotics help with the vomiting bug?
faqs.a: UKHSA says antibiotics do not work on norovirus because it is a virus, and the NHS says there is no specific medicine for it. Care focuses on rest and drinking plenty of fluids, which the CDC says replaces fluid lost through vomiting and diarrhoea. A pharmacist can supply oral rehydration powder if there are signs of dehydration, and the NHS says to call NHS 111 if fluids cannot be kept down.

faqs.q: How long is someone infectious?
faqs.a: The CDC says people are most contagious while ill and in the few days after recovering, and that studies show some people can spread the virus for two weeks or more after feeling better. UK advice from UKHSA is to stay at home, and avoid preparing food for others, until 48 hours after symptoms have stopped. The NHS gives similar advice about staying away from work, school and hospitals.

faqs.q: Do alcohol hand gels kill norovirus?
faqs.a: The NHS and the CDC both say alcohol-based hand gels do not kill norovirus. Washing hands with soap and water is the recommended measure. The CDC also advises cleaning and disinfecting contaminated surfaces, because the virus can spread when people touch contaminated surfaces and then put unwashed fingers in their mouths, as well as through direct contact.

faqs.q: Why do outbreaks happen in hospitals and care homes?
faqs.a: The CDC says health-care facilities such as hospitals and nursing homes are among the most commonly reported settings for norovirus outbreaks. It describes older adults, infants and people with weakened immune systems as being at higher risk of severe illness. For this reason, UKHSA asks people who are unwell not to visit hospitals or care homes. UK outbreak guidance describes keeping affected people apart and frequent cleaning.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of shingles and how is it diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS describes the first signs as a tingling or painful feeling in an area of skin, sometimes with a headache or feeling generally unwell. A rash usually follows a few days later, typically on one side of the body. The rash turns into itchy blisters that ooze fluid, and scabs then form where the blisters were, which may leave slight scarring. Pain can range from mild to severe. The CDC lists fever, headaches, chills and upset stomach as other symptoms that can occur.

NHS 111 Wales says the rash can sit in and around the eye and can affect sight or hearing. A clinician can usually diagnose shingles from the rash itself. The CDC notes that shingles can be harder to diagnose in children and younger adults, especially when the illness is mild.

sections.heading: What causes shingles, and can it spread to other people?
sections.body:
Shingles is caused by varicella-zoster virus, the virus behind chickenpox. After chickenpox, the virus stays dormant in the body and can reactivate later. NHS inform says shingles can affect people of all ages but is more common as people get older, especially over 50, and that people with a reduced ability to fight infections, or who take medicines that affect immunity, are also at higher risk. The CDC also names older age and weakened immune systems as risk factors.

The NHS says shingles itself cannot be passed from person to person, but someone who has never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine could catch chickenpox from a person with shingles. The CDC says this happens through direct contact with fluid from the blisters or by breathing in virus particles from them. NHS advice is to stay off work or school while the rash is oozing and cannot be covered. Scottish NHS guidance lists pregnant women who have not had chickenpox, people with weakened immune systems and babies under one month old as people to avoid direct contact with.

sections.heading: How is shingles treated, and how long does it take to heal?
sections.body:
The NHS says there is no cure for shingles, but symptoms can be eased. Antiviral tablets may be offered if a person has a weakened immune system, moderate or severe pain or rash, or a rash affecting areas beyond the chest, tummy and back. The NHS says they work best when started within 3 days of the rash appearing. The CDC says antivirals can shorten the length and severity of the illness. NHS inform says early treatment may help reduce the severity of the condition and the risk of complications.

For self-care, NHS inform describes taking paracetamol to ease pain, keeping the rash clean and dry, wearing loose-fitting clothing, using a cool damp cloth and trying calamine lotion for itching. The NHS says the rash can take up to 4 weeks to heal and that skin can stay painful for some weeks after the rash has gone, but this usually improves over time. NICE CKS says specialist advice or referral is considered for people who are immunosuppressed, with clinical judgement guiding management.

sections.heading: What complications can shingles cause, and when is urgent help needed?
sections.body:
The most common complication is postherpetic neuralgia, pain that continues after the rash has cleared. MedlinePlus says that for some people the pain lasts for years and can interfere with daily life. The CDC says the risk rises with age. NHS inform also lists infection of the rash, eye problems that can lead to sight loss, and scarring. Ramsay Hunt syndrome occurs when shingles affects the facial nerve and can cause weakness on one side of the face and sometimes hearing problems. The CDC describes pneumonia, hearing problems and brain inflammation as very rare.

NHS inform says to call NHS 111 or contact the GP practice urgently if shingles is suspected and the person is pregnant, is breastfeeding with the rash on the breasts, has a rash on the eye or nose, has changes to vision, has a severely weakened immune system, or is aged 17 or under. NHS England pharmacy guidance refers shingles near the eye with visual symptoms urgently to A&E. For other suspected cases, NHS England advises getting advice from a pharmacist or NHS 111 as soon as possible. In an emergency, such as collapse, call 999.

sections.heading: Can a vaccine prevent shingles?
sections.body:
The CDC recommends Shingrix, a recombinant zoster vaccine given as 2 doses, for adults aged 50 and older, and for adults aged 19 and older with weakened immune systems. That is US advice. The CDC says the vaccine is over 90% effective at preventing shingles and postherpetic neuralgia in adults aged 50 and older with healthy immune systems.

UKHSA says the UK programme uses Shingrix, a two-dose vaccine, because the older live vaccine Zostavax is no longer used. UKHSA describes an age-based programme for adults with healthy immune systems that is being phased in over several years. It says that from 1 September 2025 eligibility extended to everyone who is severely immunosuppressed and aged 18 and over. Because eligibility has changed over time, the NHS and UKHSA pages give the current rules.

faqs.q: Can shingles be cured?
faqs.a: The NHS says there is no cure for shingles, but symptoms can be eased. Antiviral tablets may be offered in some cases and work best when started within 3 days of the rash appearing. NHS inform says early treatment may help reduce the severity of the condition and the risk of complications. The NHS says the rash can take up to 4 weeks to heal.

faqs.q: Is shingles contagious?
faqs.a: The NHS says shingles itself cannot be passed on. However, someone who has never had chickenpox or the chickenpox vaccine could catch chickenpox from a person with shingles. The CDC says exposure is through direct contact with fluid from the blisters. NHS advice is to stay off work or school while the rash is oozing and cannot be covered.

faqs.q: Who is more likely to get shingles?
faqs.a: NHS inform says shingles can affect people of all ages but is more common as people get older, especially over 50. People with a reduced ability to fight infections, or who take medicines that affect immunity, are also at higher risk. The CDC says anyone who has had chickenpox can develop shingles.

faqs.q: What is postherpetic neuralgia?
faqs.a: The CDC describes postherpetic neuralgia as long-term nerve pain that can persist for months or years after the rash clears, and as the most common complication of shingles. The NHS says skin can stay painful for some weeks after the rash has gone, but this usually improves over time. CKS directs readers to its post-herpetic neuralgia topic if pain continues.

faqs.q: What does the NHS say about shingles in pregnancy?
faqs.a: The NHS says that if a person is pregnant and gets shingles, it is mostly mild and there is usually no risk to the person or the baby. NHS inform still lists pregnancy as a reason to call NHS 111 or contact the GP practice urgently when shingles is suspected. Local NHS guidance advises a pregnant woman who has never had chickenpox and is exposed to chickenpox or shingles to contact her midwife or GP promptly.
